forks.actual: Redbox Instant by Verizon launched commercially on March 14, 2013. Redbox withdrew on October 20, 2014 because of “a lower than anticipated subscriber base.”[^11][^12] In 2010 Coinstar’s chief executive had said Redbox would use its customers to compete with Netflix’s streaming service.[^37]
forks.whatif: Redbox had tens of thousands of kiosks and the payment cards of the people who used them, which is a customer list most streaming start-ups would have paid for. But it had no content of its own in 2013 and a parent that sold coin counting. Staying in might have bought a small subscription business. It is hard to see it buying a place beside Netflix.

forks.actual: The kiosk count was about 44,000 at the end of 2013 and still 38,379 at the end of 2021, when revenue was 85% lower (derived).[^11][^17]
forks.whatif: A network cut early to its busiest few thousand locations would have carried far lower service costs and might have run for years as a small cash business, as the last video stores do. That would have required owners who wanted a small business. Outerwall was a listed company and Apollo’s funds had bought the group at a value of $1.6 billion.[^14]

forks.actual: Redbox warned in April 2022 of substantial doubt about its future and agreed a month later to an all-share sale to Chicken Soup for the Soul Entertainment, which assumed $359.9M of its debt.[^17][^19][^22]
forks.whatif: Without a buyer Redbox would probably have gone through its own bankruptcy in 2022, two years earlier, with its staff paid and its studio contracts intact. A court-supervised sale then might have left a smaller Redbox trading. Instead its debt went onto a second company and both were liquidated.
